premise: CARRIED VERBATIM FROM THE SLICE, and unchanged by it. The server owns the data: PostgreSQL is the record and the phone is a cache. The phone reads the whole log — one conditional GET, about 85 KB — before its first frame, exactly as it reads the file today, so `logbookProvider` stays synchronous and no screen grows a loading state. Writes go to the server and wait for it; there are no offline writes and no reconciliation. Photographs live in S3-compatible object storage, uploaded straight to the bucket and read back through short-lived signed URLs, and the log carries an object id and never a URL. When the server is unavailable a write is refused rather than queued. What is not being built: multi-device conflict handling, invites, roles, password reset, email, a rendered share page, server-side preferences, and real photograph capture.

decisions.status: NEW — structural, and it is the fix for a defect that has now fired twice
decisions.title: The plan's own decisions leave the DEC- namespace. They are PD-nn.
decisions.evidence: Executed. `python3 scripts/check-plan.py` at 89fc93f: `FAIL: duplicate ids: ['DEC-79','DEC-80','DEC-81']`, exit 1 — the renumbering that fixed the collision with the rulings file created a collision inside the plan. decisions.status: NEW at v7.0; AMENDED at v7.1 by ruling DEC-82, and the amendment is the half v7.0 got wrong
decisions.title: The share flag defaults move to the client's in migration 0002 — and 0002 BACKFILLS the rows already written
decisions.evidence: v7.0's half, still true: the schema had three columns `NOT NULL DEFAULT false` against the client's `defaultSharePhotos = true`, `defaultShareNotes = true`, `defaultShareCoordinates = false`, and the upsert names none of the three, so a create took the schema's answer. THE HALF v7.0 MISSED, executed by the database lens: after the two ALTERs, pre-existing rows stay `f|f|f` while every new row reads `t|t|f`, `pg_attrdef` shows the new defaults, and nothing in the table can distinguish 'written before 0002' from 'the user turned sharing off'. v7.0 said 0002 'touches nothing else' and tested only a NEW trip, so the leg it wrote could not see this.
decisions.reasoning: Ruled at DEC-82: those rows carry a default the CLIENT NEVER HAD, so they are wrong data rather than a choice. The alternative — leave them and document it — puts a permanent, undetectable inconsistency in the one table already written, and `trips` is the one table the slice arc writes on every run. The DEFAULT still carries the create case, for v7.0's original reason: naming the columns on INSERT means an ON CONFLICT clause that sets some columns and not others in a statement whose whole point is that it sets everything, which is the shape the next person tidies into overwriting H1's switches.
decisions.consequence: 0002 is two ALTERs plus `UPDATE trips SET share_photos = true, share_notes = true`, with the reasoning in the file. `share_coordinates` is NOT touched — false is correct on both sides. THE DOWN FILE IS NOT AN INVERSE AND MUST SAY SO IN ITS OWN TEXT: putting everything back to false leaves post-0002 rows wrong in the other direction, so the down file reverts the DEFAULTs only and states that the backfilled rows are deliberately left. R4's seed makes this moot for seeded rows — it writes the values from the client document and refuses a non-empty database — so this bites exactly the trips the slice arc already wrote, which is the reason it is cheap and the reason it is not zero. THE LEG v7.0 LACKED: create a trip, apply 0002, read it back.

decisions.title: `make seed` is `cmd/seed`, a separate binary, and never a flag on `cmd/api`
decisions.evidence: internal/seed's own doc comment already says it: the command 'takes its DSN as an explicit flag rather than from the environment, so that an ambient DATABASE_URL cannot aim it at a real database by accident'. v6's S12 planned `cmd/api/seed.go`.
decisions.reasoning: A flag on the server binary puts a command that writes a whole database inside the artefact that ships, where the DSN it would use is the one already in the environment. The refusal against a non-empty log is a guard, and a guard inside a production binary is one review away from being made overridable for a good reason.

decisions.title: The asset rewrite is one named function with its own legs, and it REFUSES an unmapped locator
decisions.evidence: The census: two distinct locators across 284 photographs, and the three coverAsset columns draw from the same two.
decisions.reasoning: The alternative — a second generated fixture (DEC-52, deleted as OE-8) — makes the transformation invisible, because what you compare against is the output rather than the rule. A named function is a thing a mutation can break. And the refusal is what a substitution silently gives you instead of an error: a fixture that grew a third image would be loaded with its asset unchanged and rejected by a CHECK three layers down, with the message naming a regexp rather than a locator.

Its legs include the negative, and the error names the unmapped locator.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.0; REINFORCED at v7.1, because both lenses found things only a running system shows
decisions.title: Every step that adds a route adds its arc assertion in the SAME COMMIT

VS7's real defect (`"cityIds":null`) was found by pointing the binary at a real database, not by any of 71 mutations. AND NOW: the security lens found the share capability in the access log by running `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/l/CAPABILITY7XY` and reading `docker logs` — `{"...","path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY","status":404}` — which no unit test in this repository was ever going to print. decisions.reasoning: agent-graph-spec-V4 §6.7's second half asks for the client's hard-won LESSONS and not only its entities. This is this repository's own, learned three times now: a green suite cannot tell a guard from a decoration, and neither can a document.

The corollary the record already paid for: an ABSENCE assertion in shell is the easiest kind to write so that it cannot fail, so every new absence leg removes its output files before the request and counts a file curl never created as zero. NEW COROLLARY FROM THE SECURITY LENS: an assertion about a LOG is an absence assertion too — `grep -c token` returning 0 passes just as well when the log file is empty, so every log leg asserts a positive control line in the same run.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the database lens's first blocker, REPRODUCED INDEPENDENTLY before being adopted
decisions.title: The visits write is upsert-plus-UPWARD-offset. It is never delete-then-insert, and that is the opposite of what four documents said.
decisions.evidence: REPRODUCED HERE, on the live postgres:17 at 127.0.0.1:5434, in a scratch schema mirroring 0001's constraints. A place with two visits and one photograph filed to `v-old`; `DELETE FROM visits WHERE place_id=...` then re-INSERT of the two IDENTICAL rows in one transaction; afterwards `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | (null)`. The dangling-reference check the plan relies on answered **0**, because the reference is GONE rather than dangling. THE FIX WAS EXECUTED TOO: `UPDATE visits SET ordinal = ordinal + 1000 WHERE place_id=$1`, then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT visits_pkey DO UPDATE SET ordinal = EXCLUDED.ordinal, then DELETE the ids absent from the incoming array — ordinals swapped to `v-old 0 / v-new 1` and the photograph still read `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | v-old`. THE DOWNWARD OFFSET FAILS: `ordinal - 1000` gives `ERROR: new row for relation "visits" violates check constraint "visits_ordinal_ck"`. AND ONE MEASUREMENT NEITHER LENS MADE: across all 284 fixture photographs, `place-only: 0, visit-only: 0` — 95 have both set and 189 have neither. So the state this defect produces (place set, occasion NULL) is one the client's model has never expressed.
decisions.reasoning: Four independent instructions pointed at delete-then-insert: 0001's header mandates it in capitals, the shipped `replaceTripCities` is the pattern named as the one to copy, the prior DBA pass wrote 'the same strategy applies and the same proof covers it' about visits specifically, and v7.0's own R6 leg list said 'this is the delete-then-insert reorder'. It is safe on trip_cities, which has no referencing child; visits has one, `photos_visit_fk ... ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)`. A NO-OP RE-SEND OF AN UNCHANGED ARRAY DESTROYS THE FILING, and every guard in v7.0 is blind to it.
decisions.consequence: R6 mandates the upsert form and the upward offset, with the arithmetic in the file. The offset direction is not a preference: downward violates `visits_ordinal_ck CHECK (ordinal >= 0)` and the set-based `SET ordinal = 1 - ordinal` collides on the non-deferrable UNIQUE. The DEFERRABLE alternative was declined for 0001's own stated reason — it moves the 422 to `tx.Commit()`. THE LEG R6 LACKED: re-send an UNCHANGED visits array and assert the photograph's visitId is unchanged. And the general form goes in CLAUDE.md, because it is a class: A CASCADE THAT CLEARS A REFERENCE IS INVISIBLE TO A DANGLING-REFERENCE CHECK, so 'no dangling references' is not the same claim as 'nothing was unfiled'.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the database lens's second blocker
decisions.title: The public envelope has THREE row rules, not one, and the second is nested inside a row the first correctly publishes
decisions.evidence: Measured against the fixture the seed loads. The one trip carrying a shareLinkId is `autumn-crossing` (token `kyoto-9f2a`, sharePhotos true, shareNotes true). Re-counted here rather than carried: `fushimi-inari` holds **28 visits across four trips** — japan-2026 23, kyoto-in-may 3, winter-light 1, autumn-crossing 1 — and **1 of the 27 unshared visits carries a note**. `kibune` (9 visits, 1 shared), `nishiki` (6, 1) and `bukchon` (2, 1) are the same shape. BOTH OF v7.0's NAMED R8 LEGS PASS WHILE THIS LEAKS: `tofuku-ji` is correctly absent as a wishlist place and the other-trip Kyoto places are correctly absent — those are the two shapes the leg looks for, and they exist in the fixture, so the leg goes green.
decisions.reasoning: v7.0 stated the row filter at the `places` level only. A place accumulates visits across trips BY DESIGN — 'places belong to the city; visits belong to the trip' is the model's own sentence — so a place correctly published because it is on the shared trip carries every other trip's visits with it, their dates and their notes. shareNotes=true, so the note filter does not save it. This is v6's V4-B2 one level deeper, and the lesson is the one V4-B2 already taught: a key-set assertion feels complete and is not.
decisions.consequence: docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md states three row rules: places = distinct places having a visit ON THIS TRIP; **visits within a published place = only that place's visits whose trip_id is the shared trip**; photos and walks = trip_id. R8's leg: publish autumn-crossing and assert `fushimi-inari` comes back with exactly ONE visit and no note from another trip. THE VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE IS WORTH STATING because it is what a reader would notice before a leak: the client reads `visits.first.at` as lastVisited, so an unfiltered array makes the public page show 2027-12-06 (winter-light) as the date of a trip that ended 2027-10-02. Indexing is already right — the lens executed the join and it drives off `visits_trip_idx`.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's first blocker
decisions.title: The capability is redacted in ONE function that four call sites go through, not 'in the log'
decisions.evidence: Executed against the running container: `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/l/CAPABILITY7XY` then `docker logs` gives `{"time":"2026-08-24T02:44:06.974Z","level":"INFO","msg":"request","method":"GET","path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY","status":404,...}`. The control in the same run: `GET /v1/logbook?secret=INQUERYSTRING` logs `"path":"/v1/logbook"` with the query absent, so the query-string half works and only the half it covers is wrong. FOUR sites print `r.URL.Path`: middleware.go:177 (AccessLog), :104 (Recover), ratelimit.go:151 (RateLimit), auth_handlers.go:203 (logFailure). The attribute redactor at logging.go:71 decides on the attribute KEY, and the key here is `path`, so it can never fire.
decisions.reasoning: v7.0 wrote 'the path is REDACTED from the log' — singular — and its R8 file list touched neither middleware.go nor ratelimit.go. A worker patching AccessLog alone would believe the requirement discharged with the whole suite green. AccessLog's own doc comment defends the wrong half ('THE QUERY STRING IS NOT LOGGED … a capability lives in the URL') while DEC-10 puts the capability in the PATH. THE RATE LIMITER'S LINE IS THE SHARP ONE: it fires precisely when somebody is enumerating share tokens, so the one line written during an attack is the one recording the capability being attacked.
decisions.consequence: `httpx.LoggedPath(r)` — a sibling of `ClientKey`, rewriting `/l/{anything}` to `/l/[redacted]` — and ALL FOUR sites go through it. R8's file list gains internal/httpx/middleware.go, internal/httpx/ratelimit.go and internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go. One leg per site and A MUTATION PER SITE: a fix applied to AccessLog alone must redden three legs, or the legs are one leg wearing four names. Each log leg asserts a positive control line in the same run, because `grep -c` returning 0 passes against an empty log.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's second blocker and its fourth major, which are one design question
decisions.title: A route's response policy and its rate budget are FIELDS on Route, not a derivation the next route invalidates
decisions.evidence: Two findings, one cause. (a) v7.0 wired DEC-51's capability headers into R3 and builds the capability ROUTE in R8, five steps later, and R8's file list never touches that middleware — while DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names `GET /l/{token}` as THE motivating case. (b) routes.go:17-18 says in terms: 'The day an unauthenticated route arrives that is not a credential attempt, this becomes a sixth field rather than a derivation.' R8's public read IS that day, and v7.0's OE-10 ruled the derivation stays. Measured on the live server: NO response sets Cache-Control at all — `/healthz`, the 401s and `GET /v1/logbook` return Content-Type, X-Request-Id and Date only.
decisions.reasoning: The consequence of (a) is not cosmetic. `/l/{token}` carries no Authorization header, so RFC 9111 §3.5's shared-cache prohibition — the thing silently protecting `GET /v1/logbook` today — does not reach it. A 200 with an ETag and no Cache-Control is heuristically cacheable by any intermediary, and after 'Stop sharing' a cached envelope keeps handing out live media capabilities for as long as it survives, which unbounds the very window DEC-44 shrank to two minutes. The consequence of (b) is an availability coupling nobody chose: the public read would inherit AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN, a CREDENTIAL budget of 10/min, from the same bucket instance as register and sign-in — so one person browsing a shared trip locks everybody out of signing in.
decisions.consequence: `Route` gains `NoStore bool` and `Limit` (which limiter, not a number). The middleware is applied FROM THE TABLE, so a route's policy is declared beside its pattern and a new route cannot inherit a wrong one by silence. R8's legs: `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` present on the 200 from `/l/{token}`, with a mutation dropping each; and the public read's limit is A NUMBER with its own mutation. R3 asserts the same headers on `POST /v1/media/mint`, as DEC-51 also requires. AND THE HONEST SENTENCE R8 MUST CARRY, which ratelimit.go already carries: the public read's limit is unenforceable behind a proxy until ClientKey learns X-Forwarded-For, and Caddy is deferred to next_slice. OE-10 IS RE-EXAMINED AND STANDS: `Mutating` is still read by nothing, and two fields arriving that ARE read is not an argument for keeping a third that is not.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's third blocker
decisions.title: The content-type allowlist is enumerated HERE, the disposition is restored, and nosniff's absence is a comment rather than a gap
decisions.evidence: A three-part chain and v7.0 was missing all three at once. Grep counts over the 147 KB v7.0: `image/jpeg` 0, `heic` 0, `content-disposition` 0, `contentTypeRe` 0 — the step titled 'the content-type allowlist as a schema constraint' deferred the actual list to the worker. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` was correctly STRUCK by V4-SF3, because S3's response-header override set is closed and no presigned GET can produce it. So v7.0 kept the removal of the fallback defence and dropped the primary one. The shipped schema already accepts the payload and says so about itself: 0001:119 is `CHECK (content_type <> '')`, and its own comment at lines 95-101 calls it 'THE WEAKEST CHECK IN THIS FILE' and states that `text/html; <script>` is accepted.
decisions.reasoning: An object stored as text/html is served AS HTML from the bucket origin, at a URL the public share envelope embeds — stored XSS on the storage origin, reachable by anyone holding a share link. DEC-51 states the defence literally: 'THE DEFENCE IS THE DISPOSITION PLUS THE ^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$ ALLOWLIST, and the residual is named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered.' A list that lives in the worker's head is a list the schema constraint cannot be written against, which is why 0001's placeholder has been waiting since VS4.
decisions.consequence: `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$` written out in R3's step text, in Go for the 422 naming the field AND as a schema IN-list in migration 0003 — both, on DEC-58's precedent. `image/png` and `image/jpeg` are load-bearing beyond the fixture: schema_test.go:62 seeds shared fixtures with `content_type='image/jpeg'`, so omitting it breaks every leg using that helper. `response-content-disposition: attachment` is restored on EVERY presigned GET, with a leg. V4-SF3's nosniff reasoning is carried forward in a comment beside it so the next worker does not re-litigate a settled point. SEPARATELY, AND IT IS A QUESTION RATHER THAN A DECISION: `heic` has no producer anywhere in this system — the client's shutter is inert by decision and DEC-41 seeds two PNGs — so the allowlist could be one character shorter. That is RULE-09; DEC-51 is a ruling and this plan enumerates it as ruled.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's first major
decisions.title: The LENGTH is signed exactly as the checksum is, and the two halves fail the same way
decisions.evidence: v7.0's checksum ban is backed by a grep that CAN fail and a real-MinIO 4xx leg; the security lens calls it 'the best-specified thing in plan-v7'. The parallel size requirement has no grep, no MinIO leg, and no number: `content-length` 0 occurrences, `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` 0 occurrences, and 'the bound' is never given a value anywhere in 147 KB. DEC-51 required `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT 'so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping'.
decisions.reasoning: What v7.0 substituted — an API-side 422 before signing, plus a HEAD on commit — binds nobody. The 422 happens BEFORE the capability is minted, and the HEAD only refuses to MARK the object committed; the bytes are already in the bucket. Nothing in these eight steps reclaims them, because the sweep is explicitly out of scope. So one legitimately-minted upload URL is an unbounded, unreclaimed write. The asymmetry was invisible from the definition of done, which listed the checksum grep and the byteSize bound in one breath as though one mechanism enforced both.
decisions.consequence: `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` joins internal/config with the other eight. The length goes into the signature (minio-go's PresignHeader, or PostPolicy for the browser case). A leg mirroring the checksum one: a PUT of more bytes than were signed is refused BY THE BUCKET, and `store.Stat` errors afterwards — 'a refused PUT that still wrote something is the same defect wearing a 4xx' applies unchanged. The definition-of-done grep is extended to cover both halves so they fail together.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — from the security lens's second major
decisions.title: Revoked and unknown do the same WORK, and the leg counts calls rather than timing them
decisions.evidence: DEC-10 reads: "'Never existed' and 'revoked' are the SAME 404 WITH THE SAME WORK DONE, so nothing confirms a guessed token was once real." v7.0 carried only 'byte-identical', and its leg compares bodies and headers minus X-Request-Id. `constant-time` appears 0 times in v7.0.
decisions.reasoning: A handler that returns early on 'no row' but, for a REVOKED row, resolves the trip, checks three share flags and mints media URLs is byte-identical on the wire and still a clean timing oracle for 'this token was once real'. That is a REVOCATION oracle, not a guessing one — guessing is bounded by 31^12 ≈ 7.9e17 and is not the concern — and DEC-67's revoke-then-insert history design is exactly what makes it worth attacking. The precedent is already the strongest thing in this codebase: internal/auth/service.go's eagerly-computed dummyHash, whose leg COUNTS Verify calls rather than timing them, because a timing leg is a flake on a loaded machine and a pass on a fast one.
decisions.consequence: R8 selects the row regardless of `revoked_at` and decides afterwards, so the lookup is the only branch. Its leg counts store calls on both paths and asserts they are equal, in the shape internal/auth/service_test.go already has. v7.0's 'answer 410 for a revoked link' mutation stays — it is a good mutation — but it is no longer the only one.

decisions.status: NEW at v7.1 — and it is a conflict between two instructions that both look right
decisions.title: DEC-83's comment CANNOT go in 0001, and the paired CHECK a reader will reach for instead is unexecutable
decisions.evidence: TWO EXECUTIONS, both run here. (1) THE CHECKSUM. `loadMigrations` computes `sha256.Sum256(body)` over the whole file, comments included, and `Migrate` answers `ErrChecksumMismatch` when it moves — so a `--` comment added to 0001 breaks every database that has already applied it, including the one on 127.0.0.1:5434. DEC-83's stated consequence is 'a comment on the two columns in 0001'. (2) THE TEMPTING FIX. `CHECK ((place_id IS NULL) = (visit_id IS NULL))` — the exact shape of `photos_coordinates_paired_ck`, which sits three columns away in the same table — BREAKS D2's KEEP BRANCH OUTRIGHT. Executed on postgres:17 against a scratch schema mirroring 0001: deleting the place gives `ERROR: new row for relation "photos" violates check constraint "photos_filing_paired_ck"`, `DETAIL: Failing row contains (..., ph-1, null, v-old)`, `CONTEXT: SQL statement "UPDATE ONLY "photos" SET "place_id" = NULL ..."` — and the delete aborts, photograph unchanged. Deleting only the visit fails the same way in mirror image. The two SET NULL rules fire as two separate single-column UPDATEs, so the intermediate row is ALWAYS incoherent and any CHECK relating the two columns sees it.
decisions.reasoning: This is DEC-66's blocker recurring one layer along, and PostgreSQL echoes its own generated statement in both cases — the same signature. DEC-83 is MORE right than its own reasoning states: it declined the composite FK because that changes delete behaviour, which is a decision for the app's sheets rather than for a DBA. The cheap CHECK alternative is not a milder version of the same idea; it is unexecutable, and it is sitting in plain sight next to a constraint of identical shape that works.
decisions.consequence: The comment becomes `COMMENT ON COLUMN photos.place_id` / `photos.visit_id` in migration **0003**, which is forward-only and needs no edit to 0001 — and it is BETTER than a `--` comment for a reason that has nothing to do with the checksum: a catalog comment is readable from `\d+` and from any tool a later DBA runs, where a comment in a file nobody re-reads is not. The comment names this as the SECOND integrity rule deliberately left in Go (DEC-02's cross-kind id uniqueness is the first) AND records that the paired CHECK was executed and aborts D2's keep branch, so the next reader does not spend an afternoon rediscovering it. ONE MEASUREMENT SUPPORTS DEC-83 AND ONE COMPLICATES IT: across all 284 fixture photographs, 95 have both columns set and 189 have neither — `place-only: 0, visit-only: 0` — so the invariant is real in the data even though the schema cannot hold it, which is precisely why leaving it in Go needs a comment rather than silence.

steps.title: Migration 0002 — the share defaults the client already had, the backfill the lens found, and a lock_timeout on the runner
steps.size: SMALL, and smaller at v7.1 than at v7.0: the photograph capture is DONE (ruling DEC-77, executed at 7b47bee), so what is left is one migration with a backfill, one line in the runner, and one document.
steps.why_first: v7.0 was first for an irreversible reason and that reason has been discharged: the two PNGs are captured at `internal/logbook/testdata/imagery/`. What keeps R1 first now is smaller and still real — 0002 and 0003 are the first migrations in this project's history to touch a SHIPPED, WRITTEN table, and the database lens executed what that means: with no `lock_timeout` on the runner, an ALTER waiting behind an open REPEATABLE READ reader blocks every subsequent SELECT on `trips`, unbounded. R1 is where that line goes in, before R3 adds the second ALTER.

migrations/0002_share_defaults.down.sql   (NEW — and it is NOT an inverse; the file says so)

steps.work:
1. Migration 0002 alters `share_photos` and `share_notes` to DEFAULT true, with a comment carrying the client's own sentence about why `share_coordinates` stays false: a pin on your accommodation is not something to hand out by link, so it has to be actively turned on.
2. IT ALSO BACKFILLS (ruling DEC-82): `UPDATE trips SET share_photos = true, share_notes = true`. `share_coordinates` is not touched. The reasoning goes in the file — those rows carry a default the CLIENT NEVER HAD, so they are wrong data rather than a choice, and nothing in the table can distinguish 'written before 0002' from 'the user turned sharing off'.
3. THE DOWN FILE IS NOT AN INVERSE AND ITS OWN TEXT SAYS SO. It reverts the two DEFAULTs and deliberately leaves the backfilled rows: putting everything back to false would leave post-0002 rows wrong in the other direction. A down migration that silently does less than its up migration is worse than one that says which half it cannot undo.
4. `Migrator.Migrate` sets `lock_timeout` on the migration connection, beside the existing `set_config('search_path', …)`. One line, cheapest now while the runner is small, and it turns a migration that cannot get its lock into a loud failure rather than a stalled table.
5. 0001 IS NOT EDITED. `loadMigrations` checksums `sha256.Sum256(body)` over the whole file, comments included, so any edit — including a comment — raises `ErrChecksumMismatch` against every database that has applied it. This is stated here because ruling DEC-83 asks for a comment in 0001 and it cannot go there; PD-13 has where it goes instead.
6. docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md is created, for a reader who has NOT read this repository, and its first item is ruling DEC-76: `logbookFormatVersion` -> 2, before the first real request. Then the sign-in flow, which is two requests and a screen that does not exist; DEC-45's platform secure storage as the seventh client dependency; DEC-56's four sentences of copy; DEC-47's ImageProvider keyed by OBJECT ID rather than URL, because NetworkImage's equality is (url, scale) so a re-mint misses the cache every time; and that `assets/imagery/` is gone from wipe/mock-data, so every AssetImage in that build draws the failure plate and real media is now load-bearing rather than optional. Every later step appends to it.

steps.title: internal/media — minio-go behind one interface, a signature that covers BOTH the checksum and the length, and a third compose service
steps.size: LARGE. A new external dependency, a new compose service, and a signing call that FAILS OPEN.
files: internal/media/store.go        (NEW — PresignPut, PresignGet, Stat. NOT Remove; see OE-12)
internal/media/memory.go       (NEW — the in-memory twin, for handler-level legs)
internal/config/config.go      (EDIT — the S3_* variables and MEDIA_MAX_BYTES)
.dockerignore                  (EDIT — patterns, not two exact paths; R2 is where secrets arrive)
deploy/docker-compose.yml      (EDIT — minio, its healthcheck, its named volume)
cmd/api/main.go                (EDIT — construct the store, panic on nil at wiring time)

steps.work:
1. `media.Store` declares **PresignPut, PresignGet and Stat**, ctx first on every method. `Remove` is deliberately absent — OE-12 — because the sweep that would call it is out of scope and its shape is not knowable until the NOT EXISTS liveness query exists.
2. THE CHECKSUM BAN, and it is the sharpest thing in this step. `PresignedPutObject` and `Presign` both FAIL OPEN: reach for either and no checksum is signed, the upload succeeds, the commit's HEAD succeeds, and a lying client has written arbitrary bytes at an address claiming to be their hash. The URL is minted so the client-supplied SHA-256 is part of what the signature covers, so MinIO — and real S3 — refuse the PUT themselves.
3. **THE LENGTH IS SIGNED THE SAME WAY** (PD-11, and DEC-51 asked for it in these words: `content-length` SIGNED INTO the presigned PUT 'so the BUCKET enforces it rather than the API hoping'). v7.0 had an API-side 422 before signing plus a HEAD on commit, and neither binds the holder of the URL: the 422 happens BEFORE the capability is minted, and the HEAD only refuses to MARK the object committed — the bytes are already in the bucket, and nothing in these eight steps reclaims them. `MEDIA_MAX_BYTES` joins internal/config with the other eight variables and IT HAS A NUMBER rather than being called 'the bound'.
4. DEC-42's two addresses: `S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT` is what the API dials, `S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is what a signature covers and what a phone fetches. They may differ and DEF-02 is why. The signer only ever sees the public one.
5. DEC-47's two lifetimes: `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PRIVATE` (~2 minutes, the revocation knob) and `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC`. **THE PUBLIC ONE HAS NO NUMBER AND THIS STEP CANNOT INVENT ONE** — see RULE-07, which is a blocker on this step. It is the number D3's and H1's copy is written against.
6. MinIO joins compose as the third service — divergence 3 (DEC-39), finally reached. Its healthcheck's timeout goes strictly below its interval, because the compose file shipped violating that rule once and H3 is the leg that caught it. Its bucket is a named volume, for the reason `pgdata` is one.
7. `.dockerignore` gains PATTERNS. It currently names two exact paths — `deploy/.env` and `.env` — and no patterns, so `COPY . .` carries any `.env.local`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa` or `secrets/` into the build stage and the build cache. The existing lines were written to the shape of the file that leaked (the recorded `hunter2-vs1fixes-canary` measurement) rather than to the class, and **R2 is the step that introduces this project's first real secrets**. Add `.env.*`, `!.env.example`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa*`, `secrets/`, `.netrc`, `.aws/`.
8. Adopt the dependency only after re-running DEC-43's measurement on the ACTUAL repository rather than the throwaway module: `go mod tidy` must leave `go 1.25.0` alone and build and vet must both exit 0.

files: internal/postgres/media_store.go       (NEW — the begin upsert and the commit)
internal/httpapi/routes.go             (EDIT — three rows, and the two policy fields of PD-09)

steps.work:
1. POST /v1/media takes {sha256, byteSize, contentType} and answers {id, uploadUrl, expiresAt, alreadyExists}. `alreadyExists` derives from `uploaded_at IS NOT NULL`.
2. **THE UPSERT'S CONFLICT BRANCH IS BOUNDED**, which v7.0 never specified: `... DO UPDATE SET byte_size = EXCLUDED.byte_size, content_type = EXCLUDED.content_type WHERE media_objects.uploaded_at IS NULL`. Without the WHERE, a client re-beginning an already-committed digest rewrites the declared type and size of bytes it no longer controls — executed by the database lens: a committed row `(10 | image/png)` became `(999999 | text/html)`, and migration 0003's allowlist does not close it because any allowlisted-but-wrong type passes. With the WHERE the row is untouched.
3. **AND RECORD WHY THE DELETED `RETURNING` CANNOT COME BACK.** v6 deleted it as OE-4 with the reason 'not an xmax trick', which leaves the door open. The real reason, executed: `DO UPDATE … WHERE <false>` and `DO NOTHING` both return ZERO ROWS (`INSERT 0 0`, no row emitted), so a handler reading its answer off RETURNING gets nothing on exactly the `alreadyExists` path. A separate SELECT is correct and is race-free under `WithTravellerLock`.
4. POST /v1/media/{id}/commit HEADs the bucket, verifies the size, sets `uploaded_at`. 409 `upload_incomplete` when the object is not there. This is PD-05's first Service operation.
5. POST /v1/media/mint takes a LIST of ids and answers a list of URLs. No singular GET (OE-1), no batch store method (OE-2) — presigning is a local HMAC, so the loop is in the handler.
6. **THE ALLOWLIST IS `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$`, WRITTEN OUT HERE** (PD-10, DEC-51). v7.0 named the constraint and deferred the list to the worker, so the schema check could not be written and all three layers of the anti-XSS defence were absent at once. Enforced TWICE on DEC-58's precedent: in Go for the 422 naming the field, and as an IN-list in 0003. `image/png` and `image/jpeg` are load-bearing beyond the fixture — `schema_test.go:62` seeds shared helpers with `image/jpeg`, so omitting it breaks every leg using them. RULE-09 asks whether `heic` should be there at all; this plan enumerates DEC-51 as ruled.
7. **`response-content-disposition: attachment` ON EVERY PRESIGNED GET.** DEC-51 states the defence as the disposition PLUS the allowlist, with the residual named: a mislabelled object is downloaded, never rendered. v7.0 had neither, while keeping V4-SF3's correct removal of `nosniff` — which S3's closed response-header override set cannot produce. Carry V4-SF3's reasoning forward in a comment so it is not re-litigated.
8. **DEC-51's HEADERS ARE APPLIED FROM THE ROUTE TABLE** (PD-09), not from a path-prefix guess in middleware. `Route` gains `NoStore bool` and `Limit`. R3 asserts `Cache-Control: no-store, private` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on `POST /v1/media/mint`; R8 asserts the same on `GET /l/{token}`, which is the case DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names and which v7.0 wired into the step that does not build it.

steps.size: medium-large — six routes, of which one is a seven-row cascade and three are a privacy surface

steps.work:
1. DELETE /v1/trips/{id} implements D3's own table exactly and nothing more: the trip goes; its photographs and their notes go; its walks go; every place SURVIVES, minus that trip's visits, INCLUDING a place left with zero visits, which is a wishlist place and is what the sheet promised; the cities are untouched; the link dies because the link is on the trip. It answers the WHOLE LOGBOOK, because the cache cannot splice a cascade.
2. The server-side `_repointed`: after the cascade no surviving photograph names a visit that has gone. The schema does this through `ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)` — which exists only because the DBA found it — and the leg asserts it rather than trusting it.
3. PUT /v1/trips/{id}/share writes only the flags that were sent. POST mints a link the CLIENT supplies and revokes the current row in the SAME TRANSACTION (DEC-67). DELETE revokes AND resets all three flags EXPLICITLY to true/true/false — an UPDATE does not see a DEFAULT, so PD-01's migration does not do this for you.
4. DELETE /v1/auth/session revokes this token, **and it gains a sibling that revokes them all**. The security lens's argument is short and right: a stolen token is precisely the case where you do not know which row to delete, and 'this token' is the one thing the thief will not use. Against a thirty-day untuned TTL that is the only recovery a user has. The client has no control that calls either — which goes in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES rather than being a reason not to build them.

steps.title: Cities and places — D2's two branches, the statement order that decides one of them, and a visits write that does NOT delete-then-insert
steps.size: LARGE, and larger at v7.1: the visits write was specified wrongly by four separate documents and the correction is the step's second piece of real business logic.
steps.work:
1. PUT /v1/cities/{id} is createCity. With `attachTo` it also appends the new id to that trip's cityIds IN THE SAME TRANSACTION and is therefore CASCADING — it answers the whole logbook. Country is two columns (DEC-59) and comes from the request, because the client's geocoder supplies it and the user never types it.
2. PUT /v1/places/{id} carries the WHOLE ORDERED visits array. Ordinals are assigned from the array's position, and the array is newest-first because that is what the client sends and reads.
2b. **AND THE WRITE IS AN UPSERT, NOT A DELETE-THEN-INSERT** (PD-06). This reverses what four documents said — 0001's header mandates delete-then-insert in capitals, the shipped `replaceTripCities` is named as the pattern to copy, the prior DBA pass wrote 'the same strategy applies and the same proof covers it' about visits specifically, and v7.0's own leg list called this 'the delete-then-insert reorder'. It is safe on `trip_cities`, which has no referencing child. `visits` has one: `photos_visit_fk … ON DELETE SET NULL (visit_id)`. Reproduced on the live postgres:17 — delete a place's visits and re-insert the two IDENTICAL rows in one transaction, and the photograph filed there comes back `ph-1 | fushimi-inari | (null)`. **A NO-OP RE-SEND OF AN UNCHANGED ARRAY DESTROYS THE FILING**, silently, with no count moving and `DELETE 2 / INSERT 0 2` as the only trace. THE SHAPE, executed and verified to preserve the filing: `UPDATE visits SET ordinal = ordinal + 1000 WHERE traveller_id=$1 AND place_id=$2`, then `INSERT … ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT visits_pkey DO UPDATE SET ordinal = EXCLUDED.ordinal, …`, then DELETE only the ids absent from the incoming array. **THE OFFSET GOES UPWARD AND THAT IS NOT A PREFERENCE**: downward violates `visits_ordinal_ck CHECK (ordinal >= 0)` (executed: `new row for relation "visits" violates check constraint "visits_ordinal_ck"`), and the set-based `SET ordinal = 1 - ordinal` collides on the non-deferrable UNIQUE because it is checked per ROW during a statement. Making the constraint DEFERRABLE was declined for 0001's own stated reason: it moves the 422 to `tx.Commit()`.
3. DELETE /v1/places/{id}?photos=keep|delete — THE PARAMETER IS REQUIRED, not defaulted. A default is a silent answer to the question D2 makes the user answer on screen.
4. D2's DELETE BRANCH IS STATEMENT ORDER AND NOT A FOREIGN KEY, and this is DEC-82's second Service operation. The photographs must be deleted BEFORE the place: delete the place first and `ON DELETE SET NULL (place_id)` clears their place_id, and the delete then matches nothing. Two lines whose order silently inverts the sheet's promise.
5. D2's KEEP branch is the foreign key: the photographs lose their pin and their occasion together and keep their date and city — which is exactly `Photo.copyWith(clearPlace: true)`, and it is executable only because of the column-list form the DBA found.
6. THE WALKS ARE NOT TOUCHED. There is no place_id on walks, and that absence is D2's 'the track stays with the day it was recorded either way'. The leg asserts the walk count is unchanged on BOTH branches.

steps.title: Photographs and walks — the caption, the delete, the bulk snooze, and a re-file that honours the occasion the client chose
steps.size: LARGE — five routes, and one of them is the most intricate write in the system
steps.work:
1. PUT /v1/photos/{id} is setPhotoCaption, and it validates that `asset` names a COMMITTED object — the Go check exists to produce a 422 naming the field, and photos_asset_fk is what actually guarantees it. Empty or whitespace caption stores NULL and never the empty string, because that is what the client does.
2. DELETE /v1/photos/{id} is non-cascading: 204 and a new ETag. Nothing points at a photograph.
3. POST /v1/photos/snooze is the first route taking a COLLECTION, so it is the first place a partial failure has to answer for a group. All-or-nothing in ONE transaction with ONE version bump; an unknown photo id in the list is SKIPPED rather than fatal, matching the client's own method. An EMPTY match writes nothing and says so.
4. POST /v1/photos/{id}/refile is PD-05's third Service operation, and it VALIDATES rather than re-derives. The client mints both the placeId and, when the occasion is new, the visitId and its `at` — so the server's job is to check them, not to choose. It REFUSES a place in another city. It sets place_id and visit_id TOGETHER, always — **and ruling DEC-83 says the schema does NOT enforce that**, so the rule lives here and in the `COMMENT ON COLUMN` migration 0003 carries (PD-13). Executed: a photograph can name place P while naming a visit belonging to a different place, and the table accepts it. The paired CHECK a reader will reach for — `CHECK ((place_id IS NULL) = (visit_id IS NULL))`, the exact shape of `photos_coordinates_paired_ck` three columns away — is UNEXECUTABLE: it aborts D2's keep branch, because the two SET NULL rules fire as two separate single-column UPDATEs and the intermediate row is always incoherent. That is DEC-66's blocker recurring, and PD-13 carries the output. Ordinals are rewritten in `at` DESC, which is why visits.at is timestamptz and not date (DEC-68): the fixture visits Kyoto three times and a date column cannot break the tie.
5. PUT /v1/walks/{id} is setWalkName and dismissWalk. A dismissed walk is not a deleted walk — it keeps its points, and the read returns it.

steps.title: GET /l/{token} — the public read, against an allowlist written three steps ago
steps.size: LARGE, and it is the one step where a defect is a privacy leak rather than a bug. THREE of the five blockers the two lenses raised land here.
files: internal/httpapi/routes.go            (EDIT — one row, with NoStore and its own Limit)
internal/httpx/logpath.go             (NEW — PD-08's LoggedPath, a sibling of ClientKey)
internal/httpx/middleware.go          (EDIT — AccessLog and Recover route through LoggedPath)
internal/httpx/ratelimit.go           (EDIT — the warn line, and it is the sharp one)
steps.work:
1. GET /l/{token} resolves a share link — arriving with no traveller in hand, through the global unique index on token — and answers docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md's allowlist and nothing else. Unauthenticated, rate-limited, and the capability kept out of the log.
2. **THE REDACTION IS ONE FUNCTION AND FOUR CALL SITES GO THROUGH IT** (PD-08). v7.0 wrote 'the path is REDACTED from the log' — singular — and touched neither middleware.go nor ratelimit.go. Measured on the running container: `curl /l/CAPABILITY7XY` logs `"path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY"`. Four sites print `r.URL.Path` and the attribute redactor decides on the attribute KEY, which here is `path`, so it can never fire. `httpx.LoggedPath(r)` rewrites `/l/{anything}` to `/l/[redacted]` and AccessLog, Recover, RateLimit and logFailure all call it. **The rate limiter's line is the sharp one**: it fires precisely when somebody is enumerating tokens, so without this the one line written during an attack is the one recording the capability being attacked.
3. **THREE ROW RULES, NOT ONE** (PD-07). v7.0 filtered at the `places` level only. A place accumulates visits across trips by design, so a place correctly published because it is on the shared trip carries every other trip's visits with it — `fushimi-inari` holds 28 visits across four trips, exactly ONE of them on the shared `autumn-crossing`, and one of the other 27 carries a note. shareNotes is true on that trip, so the note filter does not save it, and BOTH of v7.0's named legs pass while it leaks. The rules: places = distinct places having a visit on THIS trip; visits within a published place = only that place's visits whose trip_id is the shared trip; photos and walks = trip_id.
4. **THE CAPABILITY HEADERS ARE ASSERTED HERE, FROM THE ROUTE TABLE** (PD-09). v7.0 wired DEC-51 into R3 and builds the route here, and R8's file list never touched that middleware — while DEC-51's own evidence paragraph names this route as the motivating case. It matters more here than anywhere: `/l/{token}` carries no Authorization header, so RFC 9111 §3.5's shared-cache prohibition — the thing silently protecting `GET /v1/logbook` — does not reach it, and a 200 with an ETag and no Cache-Control is heuristically cacheable by any intermediary. After 'Stop sharing' a cached envelope keeps handing out live media capabilities, which unbounds the window DEC-44 shrank to two minutes. Measured: NO response on the live server sets Cache-Control at all.
5. **THE PUBLIC READ GETS ITS OWN LIMITER AND ITS OWN NUMBER** (PD-09). Under v7.0's `!Auth` derivation it would inherit `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` — a CREDENTIAL budget of 10/min — from the SAME bucket instance as register and sign-in, so one person browsing a shared trip locks everybody out of signing in. routes.go:17-18 already predicted this day in its own words: 'The day an unauthenticated route arrives that is not a credential attempt, this becomes a sixth field rather than a derivation.' **AND THE HONEST SENTENCE GOES IN THE FILE**: this limit is unenforceable behind a proxy until ClientKey learns X-Forwarded-For, and Caddy is deferred to next_slice — the same sentence ratelimit.go already carries.
6. **REVOKED AND UNKNOWN DO THE SAME WORK, NOT MERELY THE SAME BYTES** (PD-12). DEC-10 says 'the SAME 404 WITH THE SAME WORK DONE'; v7.0 carried only 'byte-identical'. A handler that returns early on 'no row' but, for a revoked row, resolves the trip, checks three flags and mints URLs is byte-identical and still a clean oracle for 'this token was once real' — which DEC-67's revocation-history design makes worth attacking. Select the row regardless of `revoked_at` and decide afterwards, so the lookup is the only branch.
7. THE ALLOWLIST GUARD IS STRUCTURAL: parse, walk, assert the key set at every level EQUALS the allowlist. That is what lets a city's centre stay visible — the assertion becomes 'the only `lat` in this document is under cities[].centre', which a substring search cannot express.
8. TWO MINT SURFACES. When sharePhotos is false a signed URL must not be MINTED AT ALL — not minted and withheld — because a minted URL is a live capability whether or not it reaches the response. And every minted URL uses the PUBLIC TTL, which OE-15's replacement leg asserts by call site rather than by comparing the two numbers.
9. sharePhotos off removes `photos` entirely. shareNotes off strips Visit.note AND Photo.caption. shareCoordinates off strips Place.coordinates, Photo.coordinates, Photo.accuracyMetres AND Walk.points; the city CENTRE stays, because it is coarse and it is what a map opens on with no pins.

next_slice.what_it_is: CADDY AND THE PROXY HOP, and it is a slice rather than a chore because it is the first time a request in this system passes through something before reaching the API.
next_slice.why_it_is_first_next: httpx.ClientKey keys on RemoteAddr. That is correct for a direct connection and wrong the moment a proxy appears, at which point every request arrives from the proxy's address and the rate limiter is ONE BUCKET FOR THE WHOLE INTERNET — in front of an unauthenticated Argon2 surface costing 64 MiB per attempt and a public share read. It has been deferred twice, by the slice and by this plan, and it is now the largest single thing standing between this stack and anything a second machine can reach. The leg that settles it exists nowhere: two different X-Forwarded-For values behind ONE RemoteAddr, and separate buckets.
what_else_is_in_it: The fourth compose service, its two named volumes (without caddy_data and caddy_config, automatic HTTPS re-issues on every restart), and go_backend.md L32 finally satisfied at three services plus the fourth divergence.
DEF-01 and DEF-02: how a physical iPhone reaches the stack, and which hostname the bucket is addressed by.

The `.env.example` / compose / config.Load coverage test — one leg, and the last item on EVIDENCE.md's 'guarded by nothing' list that a single test closes. Delete ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT from the compose file today and `make check` stays green while the container refuses to start.
`-sweep-media`: the orphan sweep with its grace window, over four liveness columns rather than one (DEC-46). It has a schedule of nobody.
README, and docs/BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md ticked by a human with a device.

RULE-10's registration gate, if the human takes it: close registration after the first traveller, or gate it on an env variable. It belongs here rather than in R1-R8 because it is the step where this stack first faces something other than loopback, and because after `d5be39c` an authenticated stranger has a 600/min budget and, from R6, a `DELETE /v1/places/{id}?photos=delete`.

`media.Store.Remove` and the sweep together (OE-12). The database lens's carry-forward is the constraint to design against: with DEC-58's four foreign keys at ON DELETE RESTRICT, a single-statement `DELETE FROM media_objects` aborts the whole sweep on the first live object, so the NOT EXISTS across all four columns is load-bearing for the sweep's own liveness and not only for correctness. It is also what reclaims PD-11's refused oversized uploads, which nothing in R1-R8 does.

The three deployment items the security lens listed and correctly declined to action for a loopback stack: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` defaulting to a literal, `sslmode=disable`, and no `read_only`/`cap_drop`/`no-new-privileges` on the api service — least urgent of the three because stage 2 is already scratch with a numeric non-root user and no shell. They go on the checklist CLAUDE.md calls 'guarded by nothing but a human with a device', beside the iOS manifest flags.

`/healthz`'s unlimited `PingContext` against a pool of 8 (security lens, minor): loopback-bound today, so before anything is published either put it behind the proxy's ACL or give it a separate high-ceiling limiter — and do not fold it into the auth bucket.

`Params.check`'s missing UPPER bounds on Argon2 memory and time (security lens, minor). The gate counts slots rather than bytes, so a stored PHC encoding with `m=4194304` would allocate 4 GiB inside one slot and the ceiling the gate exists to provide would not be a memory ceiling. Only this build's own Hash writes those rows, which is why it is minor — and DEC-21's deferred tuning is exactly the moment somebody edits those numbers by hand.

`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on everything `WriteJSON` writes (security lens, minor). It is currently present only on the mux's rewritten 404/405, because stdlib `http.Error` set it before `envelopeWriter` took over — so it is on the responses nobody chose it for and absent from every response the app writes deliberately. One line, or one small `httpx.SecurityHeaders()` middleware, which is also where PD-09's headers could land if the route-table approach proves awkward.
next_slice.and_after_that: The large seed generator — internal/seed.Generate, 50,000 photographs across three travellers — and DEC-70's index question at a size where the planner's answer means something. It is deliberately LAST rather than first: the catalog leg already proves every FK child column leads an index, which is the claim that is true at any size, and the generator answers a different question that nothing is currently asking. It is also the only thing left that would make DEF-03's timeout numbers measurable.

risks.risk: R2 is the largest single increase in this project's dependency footprint and it lands in one commit. Sixteen new modules against a repository that has had twenty in total, into a package that signs capabilities.
risks.mitigation: Measured before adoption rather than after: minio-go v7.3.0 declares exactly `go 1.25.0`, tidy leaves the directive alone, build and vet exit 0. The command is in base.measured. The shipped set — as opposed to the module graph — is re-derived from the binary with `go version -m bin/api` once R2 lands, because `go list -m all` reports 235 and that number would be quoted wrongly by the next reader.

risks.risk: THE SHARPEST THING IN R2: `PresignedPutObject` and `Presign` both FAIL OPEN. Reach for either and no checksum is signed, the upload succeeds, the commit's HEAD succeeds, and the address space is poisoned by any client that lies. It looks correct through the whole of development because MinIO is a forgiving verifier.
risks.mitigation: A grep that CAN fail, in the definition of done. The checksum leg against a PINNED MinIO tag. And — this is the part that makes it evidence — the INTERMEDIATE RED is recorded: implement with PresignedPutObject first, watch the bucket return 200 for the wrong bytes, then sign the checksum. A leg written after the correct implementation cannot say it would have caught this.

risks.risk: R4's round-trip leg is the strongest leg in the plan and it is also the one most likely to be weakened rather than satisfied. Its first red will be an enormous cmp.Diff across thirty keys, six ORDER BYs and a jsonb unnest, and the tempting response is to narrow it to the fields that pass.
risks.mitigation: Paste the whole first red into EVIDENCE.md before fixing anything. It is the inventory of what had never been tested, and it is worth more as a record than as a to-do list. The per-field legs underneath it — the visits ordering, the date rendering — exist because the round trip cannot say WHICH thing broke, not so that the round trip can be replaced by them.

risks.risk: R6's statement-order defect and R7's unordered-SELECT defect are both the kind that pass a single green run. The refile mutation in particular can return the right row by luck.
risks.mitigation: `-count=10` on the refile legs and the FAILURE RATE recorded rather than a single red — the same discipline DEC-06's snapshot proof already needs, and the DBA's own measurement (1 of 8 unlocked writers succeeding) is the reason it is not paranoia.

open_rulings.severity: BLOCKER for R2 and R8 — the plan cannot be implemented without a number
open_rulings.question: What is `S3_PRESIGN_TTL_PUBLIC`? DEC-47 makes it 'THE HONEST REVOCATION WINDOW' that D3's and H1's copy must be written against; the private one is ~2 minutes and the public one is described only as 'longer'.
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: It is the single number that decides how long 'Stop sharing' is a lie, and it is the number four sentences of client copy (DEC-56) will be written against. It cannot be derived: it is a trade between a share page that stays readable below the fold and a revocation that bites. There is no page yet — a rendered share page is out of scope — so the honest framing is that this number is sized for a consumer that does not exist.
open_rulings.recommendation: Name a number and record that it is provisional, in the same tier as the Argon2 parameters and DefaultSessionTTL: asserted as a value so it cannot move unnoticed, with nothing claiming it is the right value. Fifteen minutes is defensible against a page nobody has built; so is two. What is not defensible is 'longer'.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: DEC-44 shrank the private window deliberately so that H1's plain sentence would be true enough to keep. This is the same call for the public side and it belongs to whoever writes that sentence.

open_rulings.severity: major, OPEN — and the security lens's first blocker sharpens it
open_rulings.question: DEC-10 stores the share token in PLAINTEXT. Session tokens are hashed, with a whole argued section explaining why the hash is of the raw bytes. There is no parallel argument for share tokens anywhere in CLAUDE.md or in this plan. Is plaintext still the ruling?
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: Two things have changed since DEC-10 was ruled. PD-08 measured the same token landing in the access log in plaintext — `"path":"/l/CAPABILITY7XY"` — so a live capability is currently written to disk twice, in the database and in the log. And DEC-67's history design keeps every revoked row forever, so a database dump holds every capability ever issued, live and dead, in the clear.
open_rulings.recommendation: Hashing costs the revocation-history design NOTHING: store `sha256(token)` and keep the `revoked_at` row exactly as DEC-67 has it. What it costs is `Trip.shareLinkId` round-tripping — DEC-10's actual reason for plaintext, which is that the client displays the link it minted. But the CLIENT mints the token, so the client already holds it; the server needs to recognise it, not to reproduce it. That is worth re-examining rather than inheriting.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: DEC-10 is a ruling with a stated reason, and the reason may still hold for a case I cannot see. PD-08 fixes the log; it does not fix the dump.

open_rulings.question: DEC-51's allowlist is `^image/(jpeg|png|heic)$`. Should `heic` be in it?
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: Nothing in this system can produce a HEIC. The client's shutter is inert by decision, DEC-41 seeds two PNGs, and the fixture's 284 photographs resolve to two `image/png` objects. `image/jpeg` earns its place independently of any camera: `internal/postgres/schema_test.go:62` seeds shared fixtures with it, so omitting it breaks every leg using that helper.
open_rulings.recommendation: Enumerate DEC-51's list as ruled — this plan does — and narrow it to `^image/(jpeg|png)$` only if you agree. An allowlist entry no code path can create is a format the XSS argument has to cover for nothing.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: DEC-51 is a ruling and this plan does not narrow a ruling on its own initiative. It is also the format a real iPhone capture would arrive as, so the answer may be 'keep it, the shutter is a deferred decision and not a cancelled one'.

open_rulings.severity: major, OPEN — one line, and it removes a whole question
open_rulings.question: `POST /v1/auth/register` is public and answers 409 on a duplicate — a deliberate, well-argued enumeration surface (an address's availability is a fact a sign-up form must report). Should registration close after the first traveller, or gate on an env-supplied invite?
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: Under single-user registration the 409 is nearly harmless. But the route is also how a stranger gets an authenticated account on a deployed instance — and after `d5be39c` an authenticated account has a 600/min budget, the whole write surface, and from R6 a `DELETE /v1/places/{id}?photos=delete`. The security lens raised it; the plan's own out_of_scope already says invites and roles are out, which is not the same as saying registration is open.
open_rulings.recommendation: Close it after the first traveller, or gate it on an env variable. It is one line and one leg, and it turns 'local-only target' from a deployment posture into something the code enforces. It is NOT scheduled in R1-R8; it belongs with Caddy, in the step where this stack first faces something other than loopback.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: It changes what the product is. A backend that refuses a second traveller is a single-user backend by construction, which may be exactly right and is not this plan's call.

execution.mode: One worker per step, sequential, with a review between steps. R5, R6 and R7 are mutually independent once R4 lands and may be reviewed in any order — but they are not parallel zones, because all three write to internal/httpapi/routes.go and internal/postgres, and `parallel_zones` requires disjoint sole-write paths (§3).
execution.test_first: MANDATORY, §6.7, and it is inherited from the client's own record rather than imposed: 'Test-first for new behaviour. When tests must come after — porting, integrating generated code — say so and name what gets backfilled.' Every behavioural step above carries its first failing test IN FULL and states what the red must say. A test that passes before the implementation exists is testing something else, and that is discovered now or never.
execution.write_it_and_break_it: §8, EVERY test and not only guards. A test that has never been red has never been shown to work, and a green suite cannot tell the difference. Under test-first this is nearly free — step 2 already ran it red — so the only deliberate breaks needed are for tests written against code that already works, and those are LABELLED backfill.
execution.restore_by_file_copy_never_git_checkout: The client's plans say it, this project's VS2 lost a step's implementation by ignoring it, and six of thirteen mutation results were contaminated. Against an uncommitted tree `git checkout --` no-ops on untracked files and restores tracked ones from the index, so mutations stack and a later red belongs to an earlier one — while the suite keeps going red, which looks exactly like success.
execution.a_mutation_that_did_not_change_the_file: proves nothing. Diff before running, and check the sha256 moved. One mutation in VS6 changed a comment inside a SQL string and left the suite green.
execution.note: Two things this plan asks for that are easy to skip and are the reason the last four steps are trustworthy or not. First, PD-04: the arc grows in the same commit as the route, and the reviewer's first check is `git show --stat` against scripts/slice-arc.sh. Second, the INTERMEDIATE RED in R2 — a leg written after the correct implementation cannot demonstrate that it would have caught the defect, and R2's defect is one that looks correct for the whole of development.

mechanical_invariants.rule: §6.5 — cross-references, counts, ids, step numbering and any re-derived figure are checked by CODE, as a gate. An agent's claim to have re-derived something is not evidence.
checks: Every step id referenced anywhere in this document resolves to a step in `steps`.
No id appears twice across `decisions`, `deferred_decisions`, `deletions`, `open_rulings` and `steps`.
Every `definition_of_done` entry maps to at least one step.
No step touches anything in `out_of_scope` — in particular, no step's `files` list contains a path under /Users/mattmarshall/Documents/Flutter/Travel Log.

Every step has a non-empty `test_strategy`, and every behavioural one contains an actual test body rather than a description of one.
Every acceptance check names how it could fail.

THE RULINGS FILE IS READ, NOT TRUSTED: no plan decision claims a `DEC-` id, every `DEC-` the plan cites resolves to a ruling or to v6's own list, and `base.inputs`' size and sha256 for the rulings file are RECOMPUTED rather than compared to a field. This is the check whose absence let v7.0 certify a stale hash and reuse three ruling ids while the gate reported 0 failures.

Every citation exemption names a LOCATION and carries a reason longer than a sentence, and the exemption register is not itself scanned. THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS EXEMPTED THE IDS GLOBALLY AND WAS THEREFORE A CHECK THAT COULD NOT FAIL — it passed while two real dangling citations stood in R4's file list. Scoping it to the field found them, and that is recorded because it is the seventh time an artefact check in this project has been wrong about the artefact rather than about the code.

What happened: `go_backend.md` could not be found at its named path or anywhere under $HOME; every `how_honoured` row below was marked corroborated-but-unverifiable; the human ruled 'proceed — the plan is the record'; the file then resurfaced at `sha256=e546f63d…`; and all 13 spec-sourced quotes were diffed against it mechanically, VERBATIM, with ZERO MISMATCHES. The four unquoted lines L26-L29 turned out to be a heading gap and no constraint was lost. THE UNCERTAINTY RESOLVED IN THE PLAN'S FAVOUR, and it was still worth disclosing while it stood. ONE NARROWING THAT MUST NOT DRIFT: the Trash was never searched — that attempt returned a permissions error misread as an empty result — so 'the Trash was empty' is a claim nobody established and appears nowhere. TWO NOTES from the recovered text: L28 says the deployment files are to run this **on a VPS**, so DEC-21's local-only ruling stands but the pre-deploy checklist is answering a stated REQUIREMENT rather than a precaution; and L12's approval gate is NOT CLEARED — see `sequencing.gate`.

global_constraints.quote: Use Go 1.22 or higher. Follow the Standard Go Project Layout (e.g., `cmd/api/main.go` and `internal/`).
global_constraints.how_honoured: cmd/api/main.go + internal/{config,logging,httpx,auth,logbook,postgres,media,httpapi} (DEC-71, DEC-74). go.mod `go 1.25.0`, which SATISFIES 'or higher'. The floor is a divergence from ruling 4, not from the spec (DEC-27).

global_constraints.quote: Strictly use the native `net/http` multiplexer (`http.ServeMux`). Do not use third-party routers like Chi, Gin, or Gorilla.
global_constraints.how_honoured: One *http.ServeMux built from a declared []Route slice, using method+wildcard patterns. ServeMux does all matching; the slice is a registration source, not a router (DEC-28, forced by the measured absence of pattern enumeration).

global_constraints.quote: Exclusively use `encoding/json` for payload encoding and decoding.
global_constraints.how_honoured: Two functions in internal/httpx are the only importers. DEC-26's jsonb columns marshal through the same package — one choice satisfying two constraints.

global_constraints.quote: Use the standard `database/sql` package exclusively. Do not use GORM, sqlc, or sqlx. Use `_ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"` solely as a blank import driver.
global_constraints.how_honoured: The blank import appears exactly once, in cmd/api/main.go. Hand-rolled SQL over *sql.DB. Every column is a scalar or jsonb, so no driver-specific type support is ever needed (DEC-26). Photograph bytes never touch the database at all (DEC-36).

global_constraints.quote: Explicitly configure connection pooling in `main.go` using `SetMaxOpenConns()` and `SetMaxIdleConns()`.
global_constraints.how_honoured: Both called explicitly from env, plus lifetimes. Sized together with Argon2's 64 MiB-per-login ceiling — and DEC-36's direct-to-bucket upload exists partly so multi-megabyte transfers never join that contest.

global_constraints.quote: Use the standard `context` package to handle request timeouts and pass request-scoped data.
global_constraints.how_honoured: ReadHeaderTimeout/WriteTimeout, a per-request http.TimeoutHandler whose body IS the JSON envelope (the one response the error-vocabulary sweep cannot see), ctx first on every store and objects method, request-scoped data via unexported context key types.

global_constraints.quote: Write custom validation methods on request structs using standard Go logic and the `regexp` package. No third-party validation libraries.
global_constraints.how_honoured: `Validate() *httpx.Error` on every request struct. Compiled regexps: `idRe = ^[a-z0-9-]{1,64}$` (permissive — it MUST accept `kyoto`), `sha256Re = ^[0-9a-f]{64}$`, emailRe, countryCodeRe. Ranges in plain Go.

global_constraints.quote: Implement opaque session tokens. Generate 32-byte strings via `crypto/rand`, hash them with `crypto/sha256`, and store the hashes in PostgreSQL.
global_constraints.how_honoured: crypto/rand 32 bytes -> base64.RawURLEncoding (43 chars) -> sha256 of the RAW bytes as bytea, compared with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. THREE TOKEN KINDS, THREE TREATMENTS, and CLAUDE.md states the boundary so they are never conflated: SESSION tokens are HASHED (this line); SHARE tokens are PLAINTEXT so `Trip.shareLinkId` round-trips (DEC-10); MEDIA access is a SIGNED, EXPIRING URL and is stored nowhere (DEC-37).
